candidate.answerReason: The only valid product is 27·37 = 999, up to interchanging Y and M. Thus the four digits are 2, 3, 7, and 9.

methods.label: Use the factor 37
methods.explanation:
The repeated-digit number has a useful factorization:
\[
TTT=111T=3\cdot37\cdot T.
\]
Here \(Y,M,T\) are nonzero leading digits, so the two factors are two-digit numbers and their product is at most \(999\). Because \(37\) is prime, its factor must occur in at least one of the two factors. The only two-digit multiples of \(37\) are \(37\) and \(74\).

If one factor were \(74\), then \(E=4\). The other factor would also end in \(4\), so it would be at least \(14\). But
\[
74\cdot14=1036>999,
\]
which is impossible.

Thus one factor is \(37\), so \(E=7\). Dividing the product by \(37\), the other factor equals \(3T\). As \(T\) ranges from \(1\) to \(9\), the values \(3,6,\ldots,27\) include just one number ending in \(7\): \(27\). Hence \(T=9\), and the factors are \(27\) and \(37\).

These give four distinct digits and satisfy \(27\cdot37=999\). Interchanging the factors only swaps \(Y\) and \(M\), so every valid assignment has
\[
E+M+T+Y=7+2+9+3=\boxed{21}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
